themes.name: True cost hidden in skippable panels
themes.insight: To learn what the trip really costs the traveler digs through a left-hand sidebar and a fare-class panel the flow lets you skim past, discovering the $205/$361 headline carries no carry-on, no seat and no checked bag and the real total is nearer $493 — the point at which the pricier bundled fare would have been the better buy.

quotes.text: So the $205 headline is a fare with no carry-on and no seat.
Clicking it opens a fare-class panel — this is the step people skim past
I scrolled to row 27 and there was not one free seat on this fare.
total $361.79, flagged as "typical" for this route.
that $361.79 is not what this trip costs if you're a normal traveler.
at which point the $331 "Main" fare, which includes the seat, was the better buy from the start.

themes.name: Price levers aren't the default view
themes.insight: The two controls that move price the most — shifting dates on the flexible-dates strip and re-sorting results by price instead of the default "Recommended" — are both off by default, so a traveler who touches neither can pay several times more for the same route in the same week.

quotes.text: Sep 23 was $172, my Sep 25 was $205, and Sun Sep 27 was **$1,030**.
If your dates move at all, this strip is the highest-leverage thing on the page.
Default sort is "Recommended," not price. I'd switch that.

themes.name: Return-leg screen changes the rules
themes.insight: On the return leg the traveler has to re-read the screen because it now shows price deltas instead of totals, dangles a "+$0" option that would split the booking across two airlines, and only a small warning notes that picking a fare re-prices the outbound too.

quotes.text: Prices show as *deltas* now, not totals.
that would have made it a mixed-carrier itinerary, where a delay on one airline isn't the other's problem.
so choosing a nicer fare here re-prices the outbound too.

themes.name: Upsell nudges shape the defaults
themes.insight: At each decision point the traveler has to hunt for the free or decline option: a full-screen bundle interstitial hides "No thanks" as a text link, trip insurance forces an explicit self-incriminating opt-out, and the SMS-alerts box is already checked.

quotes.text: "No thanks" is a text link under the blue button.
you must actively tick "I understand my $361.79 non-refundable flight booking won't be protected."
The SMS-alerts checkbox is pre-ticked.
Fine print: nonrefundable, $150/ticket change fee, free cancellation within 24 hours of booking.

themes.name: Cost figures contradict across steps
themes.insight: The traveler can't take any single cost figure at face value because the screens disagree — checked bags read "$95 roundtrip" in one place and "$49" per direction in another, and a "Continue without bags?" dialog wrongly states the trip has no carry-on.

quotes.text: Watch this number — the fare panel said "$49," which is per direction.
the "Continue without bags?" confirmation claims your trip has "no carry-on or checked bags," which contradicts the page above it.
It's wrong; your carry-on is included.

themes.name: Search form defaults fight the user
themes.insight: Setting up the search takes corrective work: the origin field pre-fills the wrong city from geolocation and appends rather than replaces what you type, and the traveler has to know to pick "All Airports" so nearby airports compete.

quotes.text: typing over it appends rather than replaces. I had to hit the X first.
rather than a single airport, which is what lets JFK, LGA and EWR compete in one list.

gaps: Only one participant, and an expert one who already reasons about fare classes and mixed-carrier risk; there is no evidence of how the 'normal traveler' the conclusion rests on actually behaves.
A single session on one route (NYC->ATL), one date range, one airline (JetBlue) and one booking site — no basis for claiming the pricing structure or these patterns generalize.
The walkthrough describes the checkout screen but never completes payment or reaches a confirmation, so the final booking steps and any post-purchase friction are unobserved.
No think-aloud or emotional data — this is an annotated teardown, so we don't know where the user actually hesitated, felt anxious, or nearly abandoned.
No task metrics (time, clicks, errors, completion) and no head-to-head comparison with competing sites, so every severity rating here is judgment, not measurement.
Desktop only; no mobile, tablet, or accessibility observations.
The claims that the flexible-dates strip and the sort control behave as expected are asserted from inspection, not tested.
The source contains an unexplained internal discrepancy — the return leg reads '$361.80' while the running total reads '$361.79'.
